newsitem.title: USA: NYC jobless rate worst of 20 metro areas - Hevesi.
newsitem.headline: NYC jobless rate worst of 20 metro areas - Hevesi.

text.p: New York City's jobless rate in the first quarter was the highest of 20 metropolitan areas, and while it added jobs faster than the nation, it ranked 15th in this category, city Comptroller Alan Hevesi said Wednesday.

Still, Hevesi said New York City's economy performed well in the period, noting employment climbed almost 20,000 jobs from the fourth quarter, a 1.6 percent rate that outpaced the U.S. by one percentage point.
New York City's unemployment rate gained 0.5 percentage point from the previous quarter to 9.5 percent, nearly twice the national rate of 5.3 percent, he said in a statement.

Income levels for New York City workers climbed, as shown by a 9.4 percent rise in personal income taxes from a year ago. Yet the latest increase fell short of the 12.4 percent climb seen in first quarter 1996.

And quarterly estimated tax payments fell 2.2 percent when measured with the stunning 40.6 percent increase seen in 1996. A financial source said the drop appeared to stem from the stock market's correction in the first quarter, which likely cut capital gains tax collections.

The source, who declined to be named, added that more quarterly data were needed to assess whether this trend will persist, though he noted the stock market has rebounded, which could boost how much the city gets from capital gains taxes.
Average hourly wages climbed, especially for banking employees, whose pay rose 8.1 percent to $16.17 an hour from the year-ago period.
New York City's job gains looked striking when measured against the year-ago period, as there were 51,300 more positions than in the year-ago period.

But the city barely outperformed Newark, N.J., whose 1.5 percent rate was only 0.1 percentage point below the city's rate. The Seattle metropolitan area, where Microsoft Corp and Boeing Co are based, added the most jobs of the 20 metropolitan areas measured, achieving a 5.0 percent rate.

One bright spot for New York City's economy was tourism, as hotels saw a 76.6 percent occupancy rate in the first quarter, 4.6 percent above a year-ago. That helped hotels raise prices, with the daily room rate climbing to about $173 from $158.

The real estate market for apartments also saw some vacancy rates falling, with the yardstick for class-A properties down to 10.8 percent from the 14.6 percent level seen a year-ago. However, landlords got a bit less for their rentals, as they charged an annual rental rate of about $32 a square foot, down two dollars.

Overall inflation stayed tame, slipping 0.3 percentage point from the previous quarter to 2.6 percent. However, two sectors saw big rises: prices for medical care services shot up 5.6 percent, while energy prices gained 4.9 percent.

The city's gross domestic product (GDP) climbed at an annualized rate of 3.8 percent in the first quarter, exceeding the previous quarter's 3.4 percent gain. Hevesi said that while this was healthy growth, the city lagged the nation, whose GDP surged 5.6 percent.

Leading indicators also painted a slightly rosier picture, with claims for unemployment insurance falling by 1,586 to 32,022 in the first quarter from 1996's fourth quarter. A help-wanted index rose 4.3 percent to a 54.3 percent average. And 15,285 building permits were authorized, an increase of 1,654.
